name: Flutamide

lead: Flutamide is a prescription antiandrogen approved for prostate cancer. It has also been used off-label in women for excess hair growth, acne and hair thinning.
Evidence for scalp hair is thin, and guidelines rank it behind other antiandrogens because of liver risk.

paras: It blocks androgen receptors, so testosterone and DHT have less effect on follicles and oil glands.
Boxed warning for severe, sometimes fatal liver injury; also fetal toxicity, methemoglobinemia, hot flashes and sexual side effects in men.

lead: Flutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen that blocks the androgen receptor. It was the first drug of its type approved in the US, in 1989, for prostate cancer, and its labelled use is in combination with an LHRH agonist for locally confined and metastatic prostate carcinoma [1][2]. Its label carries a boxed warning for liver injury and says it is for use only in men [2].

Off-label, flutamide has been used in women for hirsutism, acne and female pattern hair loss, and discussed in androgen-focused forum circles as a hair-related antiandrogen [1][3][4]. A French review of antiandrogen treatments placed flutamide as third-line therapy for severe hirsutism in women, noting no market authorisation for that use [3]. Published evidence for scalp hair loss is limited; a 2023 AGA review noted only finasteride and minoxidil are FDA-approved for androgenetic alopecia [5].
infobox: Oral (a topical gel is mentioned in forums)

paras: The US label indicates flutamide with LHRH agonists such as goserelin for stage B2-C prostate cancer, started before radiation, and for stage D2 metastatic carcinoma [2]. Earlier trials examined combined androgen blockade, including leuprolide with or without flutamide and orchiectomy with or without flutamide [6][7][8]; a 1990 review covers clinical applications of antiandrogens [9].

Flutamide has been used off-label for hyperandrogenic skin and hair conditions in women, including hirsutism, acne and female pattern hair loss, because it blocks androgen action in follicles and sebaceous glands [1]. A review of antiandrogens ranks cyproterone acetate with an oral contraceptive first-line for moderate to severe hirsutism, spironolactone second-line, and flutamide or finasteride third-line only [3]. A Canadian consensus on AGA did not list flutamide among interventions recommended [10].

A general reference reports reductions of 50 to 70 percent in Ferriman-Gallwey scores after 6 to 12 months with low-dose flutamide in hirsutism studies [1]. For hair loss on the scalp no trials were identified in the sources reviewed; reviews of AGA and the Canadian consensus did not present flutamide as a standard option [5][10].

The boxed warning describes hospitalisation and rare deaths from liver failure, with about half of cases within the first three months, and recommends measuring transaminases before starting [2]. The label also warns of fetal toxicity and aniline-related toxicities including methemoglobinemia, hemolytic anemia and cholestatic jaundice [2]; methemoglobinemia has been reported in a case report [11]. A general reference reports hot flashes in over half of patients, reduced libido and impotence [1].
A T Nation poster in a 2009 thread on androgen-receptor hair loss said bicalutamide and flutamide carry more side effects orally, and that flutamide is recommended against [12].

Flutamide and its active metabolite block the androgen receptor, and it is metabolised mainly by CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 with a half-life of about 6 hours [1]. Prostate cancer research has examined androgen-receptor mutations that arise under androgen antagonist treatment [13].

Discussion appears mainly on T Nation, where flutamide is mentioned with anabolic compounds and hair loss questions. A 2003 post advised that a prescription could give access to flutamide gel, described as better than topical spironolactone [14]. The sources reviewed contain no looksmax.org threads on flutamide.

Trials in prostate cancer are extensive, including combined androgen blockade trials with leuprolide and orchiectomy [6][7][8]. For hirsutism in women, reviews summarise studies, with flutamide listed as third-line [3][8]. No published trial of flutamide for male pattern hair loss was identified.

lore.intro: Flutamide appears sparingly in forums as an antiandrogen, usually in hair-loss or androgen-receptor discussions on T Nation [12][14].

claims.claim: Topical flutamide is a stronger anti-hair-loss option than topical spironolactone.
Oral flutamide is a hair-loss option but carries more side effects than other antiandrogens.

timeline.event: FDA approves flutamide for prostate cancer; leuprolide plus flutamide trial published [1][6].
